There just haven’t been enough games like Saturday’s for the Cubs this year. It wasn’t easy. It never is with this team if they aren’t scoring 10 plus runs. But the pitching was really good save for one rough inning in the fifth that probably wasn’t as bad as it looked, aided by a weird, bad throw from Dansby Swanson on a relay play. That led to one of the two runs that the Cubs did allow in this one to being unearned. Daniel Palencia followed and was terrific. Aaron Civale was a little shaky. Ryan Zeferjahn is really tough to watch despite clearly immense talent. I’ve not followed his career and haven’t dug into it, but without doing so, I can confidently say that every coach he’s ever has dreamed of a fully unlocked Zeferjahn who might be a truly elite pitcher. Ryan Rolison faced one batter, doing his job and recording a save.
Fun fact, this team has allowed exactly two runs 34 times this year. They are 26-8 (.765) when they do so. I was surprised it was so many games, given the struggles of this pitching staff. They’ve allowed two or fewer 50 times. They have a record of 42-8 in those games. If you mentally shed a tear for this team not having a healthy dose of 2024 Justin Steele, 2025 Cade Horton or 2026 Ben Brown, this is why. I heard it said on the Marquee pregame Saturday that this position player group should have led to a 100-plus win team. It felt so bold. But it’s totally true. With reasonable pitching, this is a 100-plus win team. And that’s why the postseason is not completely hopeless. If they get some pitching, they can win.
On the other side of the ball, the Cubs turned eight hits and three walks and a hit batter into five runs. So slightly less traffic than the night before, but one more run. Two homers and not one. A double to go with it. But more than anything, it was just clustering things together a little better. For the second straight night, the Cubs got largely nothing out of the duo of Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman, who have led the way for this team, particularly in the second half. The rest of the lineup was pretty balanced and the offense was a team effort.
It’s been a week now since the last double-digit offensive game. It’s probably not worth a lot of mention, but it seems like the Cubs get one of those every week or 10 days. So that’s probably coming somewhere in the near term. It would be nice to get one of those easier ones and not to have to sweat every inning as this team closes in on clinching a playoff spot and tries to secure the top Wild Card. Regardless, the Cubs will have a chance to win a third straight series on Sunday afternoon and that’s what you want to see. It’s been a welcome bounceback after the nightmare in Milwaukee. As I said following that last game there, this team is very professional. They’ll bounce back and this won’t linger. It was a really good time to be right.
With any luck, this team will just keep on winning series as the season winds down. Win Sunday afternoon, get home and take a series from a Marlins team that is fighting down to the wire despite being eliminated. The Marlins are in San Diego and we’ll catch them coming back east after playing there and in Arizona. That’s a tough trip. Especially when the clock strikes midnight on your season mid trip. Nine-game trips are always hard. But three good teams, a couple of different time zones (that are both different from their home time zone), different styles of play. It’s a lot. Then the Cubs get a Red Sox team that is pretty squarely locked into the second Wild Card spot. They’ll want to be lining up pitching for their Wild Card series which very likely will be against the Yankees. Of course, the Cubs will be getting theirs set too. But the gap between one and six for Cub starters just isn’t massive (which is damning with faint praise).
Anyway, it was a good night in Cincinnati. Seiya Suzuki seems to be coming out of a slump a little bit. Three singles in the last two games. Only one really hit hard, but using the field and having some success. Michael Busch hit a monster homer. Dansby Swanson had his rehab washed out, but save for the weird throw, he looked like he’s ready to contribute. He had a single and a homer of his own. Good to get Dansby back. It’s his defense that provides most of his value. But, Dansby has the mind and approach of a superstar. He doesn’t shy from the biggest moments. That’s not a bad bat to have down at eight or nine in your lineup. This team is better with Dansby on the field. Just as it usually is with Ian Happ on the field. A player need not be a Superstar to produce consistent positive value for a team.
Three Positives:
- Daniel Palencia faced six batters in the sixth and seventh inning. That sixth inning was huge with just a one-run lead and the 2-3-4 hitters due up for the Reds. He was fairly efficient and got a second inning of work. He’s looked better the last couple of times and is maybe re-finding himself just in time.
- Dansby Swanson had a single and a homer, scored twice.
- Michael Busch had a single, a homer and was hit by a pitch. He scored once. He had a really nice homestand before this trip (.316/.417/.526). He hasn’t really hit a groove all year long. Maybe he too is hitting his peak at just the right time?

Scoreboard Watching: The Phillies lost for the second straight night. They fall one game behind the Cubs, while the Padres won and are tied with the Cubs. The Cubs hold tiebreakers over both teams. The Diamondbacks won a game started by Cam Schlittler, finding some offense against him and then walking it off to win. The Arizona win delays the eventual Cub playoff clinch. That’s two this week as they try to keep their very narrow playoff hopes alive. Even with the win, they remain four games behind the Phillies for the last playoff spot.
Up Next: The Cubs finish the series with the Reds. David Peterson (8-8, 5.11) starts for the Cubs. David is 2-1 with a 4.31 over his last seven, including a win last time against the Braves, allowing a run on three hits and three walks over six innings. The general trend for Peterson is about four good starts to every bad one and they are very stratified. So once he gets it going, he usually delivers. Look to see if he can get locked in early in Cincy. Certainly a guy who likes to keep the ball down is a welcome choice in that park. He held the Reds to two runs over five at Wrigley at the end of August. But they also saw him twice as a Met and did quite well against him (nine runs in eight innings of work).
24-year-old Rhett Lowder (6-11, 5.79) has had a rough first full year as a starter (27 appearances, 24 starts). The strain of a long season may be weighing him down as the year draws towards a close. He’s 2-4 with a 7.13 over his last seven games. He’s allowed 45 hits and 12 walks in just 35.1 innings over those seven starts. The Cubs have seen him twice as a starter and once as a reliever. As a starter, he’s allowed six runs in just eight innings of work. The two relief innings were scoreless, though he issued two walks. He and Peterson faced each other in that game in August. Lowder won, despite allowing three runs over five innings. He did a good job that night staying in the strike zone, not walking anyone (the only time he’s done so since July). He hasn’t won since that start at the end of August, losing all three starts (Brewers, Dodgers, Dodgers, ouch).
Get the offense going early and see if you can post some crooked numbers and ride that to a win. Don’t let Lowder settle in and find some of what made him a 7th overall pick in 2023. He’ll probably eventually be a good starter. But how about not now?

It felt like Roman Anthony was an instant star for the Boston Red Sox upon his call-up last season, but the truth of the matter was that it took a while for the hot-shot youngster to truly get going. Over his first 15 major league games, Anthony hit just .114/.291/.272.
The end result was a .292/.396/.463 performance over 71 games. We weren't complaining. It looked like the Red Sox had a perennial All-Star on their hands. Yet, thinking back on those first few games, it might have been the start of a trend.
It's not uncommon for even the best prospects to initially struggle during the first few games of their big league debut, but what has gone on since makes it seem like there's more than meets the eye.
Anthony started 2026 in a miserable slump, hitting just .229/.354/.321 before his finger ligament injury. That almost doesn't tell the whole story, though. The 22-year-old began to turn it on once the calendar flipped to May, with five hits and two walks over 15 plate appearances before landing on the IL.
The Red Sox better hope that Roman Anthony is just a slow starter and that he'll get in gear in time for October
After missing nearly four months, it was as if the youngster was starting his season again from scratch. Initially, he hit the ground running going 10-for-22 over his first five games back. But then he hit a wall. Over his last 11 games, Anthony is hitting just .149/.216/.213. His eagle eye at the plate has disappeared with just a 7.8% walk rate during that span, compared to an alarming 35.3% K-rate.
The struggles have led to calls for him to be dropped lower in the lineup. That might be a temporary solution, but even more important is that he snaps out of his funk soon.
Plenty of players throughout baseball history have gotten off to slow starts only to rebound; some have even made slow starts a habit throughout their careers. Habitually starting off behind the eight ball isn't ideal, but in the grand scheme of things, it's not catastrophic, either.
2026 saw plenty of prominent players get off to ice cold starts. Fernando Tatis Jr. didn't hit until nearly June. Old friend Alex Bregman looked washed with the Chicago Cubs before turning on the jets in the second half. Caleb Durbin no longer looks like a tragic mistake (September struggles, notwithstanding).
Given how long Anthony was on the shelf, it's almost as if he has had two Opening Days. If he truly is a chronically slow starter, that explains away the issues we're currently seeing. He's certainly not worried about it.
“I’m right where I want to be… I came back with enough time to get a good number of plate appearances, and to fail like I am right now and to succeed like I did in the beginning, and then kind of meet in the middle… [The playoffs are] what you play for after such a long year… At the end of the day, those few weeks are the only thing that really matters,” Anthony said.
It almost sounds as if Anthony was planning on this being a process, with the goal of getting back on track for the playoffs. Now, he'll have to make sure that comes to fruition; otherwise, the Red Sox will be in rough shape once the postseason rolls around.

Cubs infielder Alex Bregman's horse wins at Churchill Downs, then gets claimed by new owners
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (AP) — Alex Bregman and his Chicago Cubs teammates celebrated the third baseman's horse winning a race at Churchill Downs.
It was short-lived, however, when the horse was claimed by new owners afterward.
Act of Parliament overcame a troubled start under jockey Axel Concepcion and rallied to win by three-quarters of a length on Thursday. The 3-year-old colt paid $8.68 to win.
"It was electric,” winning trainer Will Walden said. “To have Alex and the entire team here and then have the horse come through like that made it a pretty special night.”
The Cubs visited the historic Louisville track on their off day before opening a three-game set at Cincinnati on Friday.
Cubs MVP candidate Pete Crow-Armstrong delivered a pep talk to Act of Parliament in the paddock before the race. Cubs manager Craig Counsell led the colt into the winner's circle afterward.
Several Cubs rookies dressed in racing-themed costumes, including pitcher Ryan Rolison, who donned a horse costume, and Pedro Ramirez, who dressed as a jockey.
Bregman Family Racing, the ballplayer's stable, bought Act of Parliament for $65,000.
The colt earned $27,108 for his first career victory. But Bregman lost him in the claiming race.
Act of Parliament was claimed for $20,000 afterward in a random blind draw used to break a tie when six different owners submitted bids beforehand to buy the colt. He was then transferred to a new trainer.

The Wild Card isn't the only race the Chicago Cubs are winning.
With an off-day on Thursday, the Cubs flew down to Louisville, Kentucky, to support one of their marquee players. Alex Bregman's horse, Act of Parliament, took the track at the famous Churchill Downs, and the rest is history!
Led by jockey Axel Concepcion, Bregman's horse came away victorious. And it's safe to say his Cubs teammates were thrilled to be in attendance.
Numerous posts on social media show the Cubs going absolutely bonkers for Bregman. An enormous huddle formed in the winner's circle, where Concepcion was tossed sky-high. Speaking of which, high fives were aplenty!
Even the typically stoic Craig Counsell couldn't help but jump around like a kid.
Craig Counsell in the middle of it going nuts https://t.co/QLyTogEG1u
- Brett Taylor (@Brett_A_Taylor) September 18, 2026
To make matters more fun, it appears as if several were dressed for the occasion. This included some Debry-inspired garb, but some players went as far as sporting their own jockey outfits.
Ryan Rolison decided to take a step further, though, channeling his inner horse.
Alex Bregman also shared a video on Instagram of Pete Crow-Armstrong meeting with his horse before the race. As the Cubs' likely NL MVP can be seen petting Act of Parliament, Bregman included a caption that read, "PCA pep talk we couldn't lose."
Bregman might want to consider bringing Crow-Armstrong to all his races from now on. Have you seen the last few months?
Alex Bregman's Instagram story shows the Cubs dressed up for a night at the racetrack on their flight and Pete Crow-Armstrong petting one of the ponies and giving it a "pep talk" pic.twitter.com/OOsnrmmwnN
- Josh Frydman (@Josh_Frydman) September 18, 2026
A Cubs Bonding Moment Before the Stretch Run
As silly as it may sound, a moment like that could prove to be a lot more than just a fun memory for this Chicago Cubs team.
Team morale has likely been rocked in recent weeks as they officially lost their footing in the NL Central race. Even more troubling, the Cubs have watched their sizeable Wild Card lead shrink thanks to a late-season surge from the Philadelphia Phillies. While they maintain the No. 1 spot at this point in time, they only have their regular-season tiebreaker to thank for that. Both teams are neck-and-neck with an 85-68 record on the season.
This means the Cubs' final nine games of the 2026 campaign are going to hold tremendous weight. You never quite know how a team will respond to that kind of pressure, but who's to say Thursday's party at Churchill Downs can't serve as the momentum boost they need!
Bregman's horse walking away victorious also feels poetic. The veteran struggled for much of the season, only to catch his rhythm at the perfect time. He's now looked like exactly the star the Cubs thought they were signing to a five-year deal this offseason. Over his last month of action, Bregman has slashed .313/.394/.670. In his last seven games alone, he has nine hits, two homers, and six RBIs.
Everything is coming up Bregman, and the Cubs sure hope that continues over the next several weeks!

The Chicago Cubs were off on Thursday. That doesn't mean they didn't have something to win.
With the team about to begin a road series against the Cincinnati Reds, the entire roster seemingly opted to hop the Ohio-Kentucky border and travel to Churchill Downs, where Alex Bregman's horse Act of Parliament was competing in the final race of the slate.
Act of Parliament won a thriller, starting near the back of the park and slowly making up ground on the outside, then erasing a length-plus gap in the final stretch for the win.
You can see the team cheering him on here, via video from trainer William Walden:
The Cubs players were fully invested. Bregman posting pictures on his Instagram story of multiple teammates wearing jockey uniforms on the team plane, as well as video of Pete Crow-Armstrong meeting the horse before the race with the caption "PCA pep talk we couldn't lose," which can only help the MVP campaign.
The team celebrated raucously after Act of Parliament crossed the finish line, later hoisting jockey Axel Concepcion on their shoulders.
Via MLB.com, Bregman has been a horse racing fan his entire life, something he takes from his family, and made a formal entry into the world when he opened Bregman Family Racing in 2021 alongside his wife Reagan, who also grew up racing horses.
Bregman Family Racing has seen its horses record a total of 90 starts since then.
Act of Parliament's win paid out $8.68 off a $2 bet to win and earned Bregman a $27,108 prize per Bloodhorse.
However, that appears to be the end of Bregman's association with the horse, as it was a maiden claiming race, in which all of the horses were up for immediate sale. According to Equibase, Act of Parliament was one of five horses claimed by a new set of owners at a price of $20,000 each.
With a horse racing win under their belt, the Cubs have nine games left to play in the regular season. Their record currently sits at 85-68, tied with the Philadelphia Phillies for the top wild-card spot (Chicago owns the tiebreaker) and have a five-game cushion over the Arizona Diamondbacks to make the playoffs.
If the playoff picture holds, they will host the Phillies in the NL wild-card round.

The Cubs took advantage of the Braves deciding to save their ace Chris Sale for their weekend series against the Astros.
Instead, Atlanta sent minor-league callup J.R. Ritchie to face the Cubs. The Cubs had hit Ritchie pretty well when they faced him in Atlanta in May and they did so again Wednesday evening at Wrigley Field, touching him up for seven hits and six runs in 4.2 innings on their way to an 8-4 victory, taking the series two games to one. The game featured 12 Cubs hits, including Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman both hitting triples and home runs.
Once again, a Cubs starter struggled through the first inning. Shōta Imanaga allowed two hits but no runs in a 20-pitch first, but then he really settled down. More on this in a bit.
The Cubs got their offense going in the bottom of the first. PCA led off with a walk, but was erased when Seiya Suzuki hit into a double play. Michael Busch then also walked. He scored on this double by Bregman [VIDEO].
Your browser does not support the video tag.
As you can see in the clip, Bregman got caught between second and third and was tagged out to end the inning.
Imanaga allowed a freak single with one out in the second when a ground ball that Bregman was about to field hit third base. After that, though, Shōta retired 11 Braves in a row before a leadoff double by Ronald Acuña Jr. in the sixth.
While all that was going on, the Cubs were posting a solid lead in the game. The 1-0 lead became 2-0 on PCA's 43rd homer leading off the third [VIDEO].
Your browser does not support the video tag.
That home run established a new Cubs franchise record for home runs in a season by a left-handed hitter, eclipsing Billy Williams' 42 in 1970. And I can imagine no one was cheering louder for PCA's record-breaker than Billy himself.
Another solo homer leading off the fourth made it 3-0. It was Bregman's 26th of the year [VIDEO].
Your browser does not support the video tag.
Then the Cubs blew the game open off Ritchie in the fifth. With one out, Carson Kelly singled.
Your browser does not support the video tag.
On the next pitch, Suzuki got plunked. The crowd booed, though it almost certainly was not retaliation, just a young pitcher being wild. Busch struck out, but Bregman followed with the Cubs' second triple of the inning, making it 6-0 [VIDEO].
Your browser does not support the video tag.
That got me to wondering when was the last time the Cubs had two triples in an inning at Wrigley, so I asked BCB's JohnW53 to look this up. It had been 15 years. Some of these names will amuse you:
The Cubs last hit two triples in the same inning at Wrigley Field in 2011— twice, both vs. the Cardinals:
May 11, fifth: Carlos Pena single, Starlin Castro triple, Alfonso Soriano single, Koyie Hill triple. Tyler Colvin groundout scored Hill to give Cubs 10-1 lead. They won, 11-4.
Aug. 19, seventh: Soriano groundout, Darwin Barney triple, pinch hitter Blake DeWitt triple to cut deficit to 4-3. Castro struck out and Reed Johnson grounded out. Cubs walked it off in 10th on one-out single by pinch hitter Tyler Colvin.
Tonight's game was the Cubs' 1,181th at Wrigley since Aug. 19, 2011.
Back to Imanaga's game. He allowed a leadoff double to Acuña in the sixth, and Acuña scored on a couple of ground outs. But Shōta finished off that inning with a strikeout of Ozzie Albies, his eighth K of the night on his 100th pitch, an excellent outing in which he didn't walk anyone and didn't allow any home runs.
Your browser does not support the video tag.
Your browser does not support the video tag.
Imanaga has thrown well over his last three starts: 2.00 ERA, 0.778 WHIP, 16 strikeouts and only two walks in 18 innings, with just two home runs allowed. If he keeps this up over what will probably be two more regular-season starts, he's got to be considered for a postseason start as well.
Your browser does not support the video tag.
Aaron Civale relieved Imanaga and allowed a run in the seventh, which the Cub got back in the bottom of the inning on PCA's 44th long ball of 2026 [VIDEO].
Your browser does not support the video tag.
Later in that inning, Bregman came to bat with a chance to hit for the cycle — he needed just a single. Unfortunately, he flied to center to end the seventh.
The Cubs completed their scoring for the evening in the eighth. Tyrone Taylor led off with a double and one out later scored on this single by Michael Conforto [VIDEO].
Your browser does not support the video tag.
The Cubs loaded the bases on singles by Pedro Ramirez and Kelly, but PCA struck out and Suzuki grounded out to end the inning.
Here's where I'm going to open the complaint department door just a bit. Ryan Rolison began the ninth by issuing a walk and allowing a hit, which prompted Craig Counsell to call on Ryan Zeferjahn, who immediately gave up a two-run double to Mauricio Dubon.
I mean… when you have a six-run lead, it should be easier than that to protect. Fortunately, Zeferjahn retired the next three Braves in order to end the game. Here's the final out [VIDEO].
Your browser does not support the video tag.
A couple more game notes from John:
This is just the third time in their last 15 games that the Cubs have hit multiple home runs. They have hit a total of 15. The 15-game span began Sept. 1, the day after they hit a team-record nine vs. the Brewers.
The Cubs have hit three homers in 20 games and more than three in 20 more. They have hit two in 35 games, one in 55 and none in 42.
…..
Pete Crow-Armstrong's game tonight was the 18th since 1901 in which a Cub hit at least one triple and at least two home runs. In all games, the players had one and two.
PCA is the second Cub to turn the trick twice, joining Billy Williams. PCA did it April 13, 2025, at Los Angeles vs. the Dodgers. Williams did it June 17, 1964, and May 19, 1971, vs. the Giants, both at Wrigley Field.
The one-timers: Heinie Zimmerman (1910), Bill Nicholson (1944), Hank Sauer (1949), Walt Moryn (1956), Lou Brock (1963), Leon Durham (1982), Andre Dawson (1987), Shawon Dunston (1989), Todd Walker (1989), Kris Bryant (2017), Kyle Schwarber (2017), Seiya Suzuki (2024), Michael Busch (2025) and Dansby Swanson (2025)
Games like this should remove all doubt about PCA being voted NL MVP. The only question that remains, I think: Will that vote be unanimous? It really should, especially since the two-homer game put the Cubs center fielder just one home run behind Phillies DH Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead. PCA is also now at 9.6 bWAR for the season, which gives him a chance to be just the fourth Cubs position player to ever have a 10 bWAR season (he's already there per Fangraphs, which has him at 10.4 fWAR).

CHICAGO – Pete Crow-Armstrong has joked in the past that he has not put up the best numbers when the Wrigley Field crowd unites in chanting his initials. That perceived trend has not continued with the new chants that roar through the Friendly Confines these days.
When Crow-Armstrong was in the batter’s box in the seventh inning Wednesday night, the calls of “M-V-P! M-V-P!” were already gathering steam. A few seconds later, as the Cubs’ star center fielder rounded the bases after his second home run of the evening, the repetitive cries had become deafening.
In an 8-4 victory over the Braves, Crow-Armstrong continued his assault on the Cubs’ record book and further padded his case to take home the National League’s Most Valuable Player trophy after this incredible campaign. He had a familiar sidekick in Alex Bregman, who finished a single short of the cycle to also help back a quality start from Shota Imanaga.
With the win, the Cubs maintained their half-game lead over the Phillies for the NL’s top Wild Card spot. That said, Chicago owns the tiebreaker over Philadelphia by winning the season series, taking six of seven games against the Phillies in April.
Crow-Armstrong’s two home runs pushed him past Cubs icon and Hall of Famer Billy Williams for the most homers by a left-handed hitter in team history. Williams launched 42 in 1970. Crow-Armstrong added an RBI triple, giving him 81 extra-base hits on the season. That also topped Williams’ single-season club record in that category (80 in 1970) for a lefty batter.
Per MLB.com’s Sarah Langs, this marked the 10th time in Crow-Armstrong’s career that he has collected at least 10 total bases in a game. That is now three more such games than any other player before turning 25 years old, dating back to at least 1900. Only Williams and Sammy Sosa (12 apiece) have more in a Cubs career.
Crow-Armstrong has also tied Nelson Cruz (six in 2019) for the most games with at least 10 total bases in a single season in MLB history, since at least 1900.
Entering play on Wednesday, Crow-Armstrong (4.0) and Bregman (3.1) ranked first and third in the Majors, respectively, during the second half in WAR, per Fangraphs. They have been arguably the top one-two punch in baseball for the past few months and were at it again in the win over the Braves, who are trying to secure the NL East title.
Bregman got the Cubs’ lineup rolling with an RBI double off JR Ritchie in the first inning. Crow-Armstrong then launched his 43rd homer of the season in the third. Bregman followed suit with a leadoff homer (his 26th blast of the year) in the fourth against Ritchie. In the fifth, both Crow-Armstrong and Bregman delivered run-scoring triples to help Chicago pull away.

Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman made MLB history on Wednesday night while leading the Chicago Cubs to a blowout win over the Atlanta Braves.
Crow-Armstrong and Bregman each had a home run, each had a triple and each had three extra-base hits in the 8-4 rout at Wrigley Field. That made them the first pair of MLB teammates to do that in the same game in nearly 70 years.
The last pair of teammates to pull that feat off was Willie Mays and Daryl Spencer for the San Francisco Giants in 1958, according to OptaStats.
Bregman came just short of hitting for the cycle in the win. He hit an RBI double in the opening inning to put the Cubs on the board first, and then got his solo homer in the fourth.
The best shot, though, came in the fifth. Bregman hit a two-RBI triple that just barely made it past Braves third baseman Austin Riley up the line. That put the Cubs up 6-0 at the time.
Crow-Armstrong got his home run first, also a solo shot in the third inning. He hit a second solo home run the seventh, too, and hit an RBI triple in the fifth inning just two batters ahead of Bregman.
The Braves added two runs in the ninth inning, off of a Mauricio Dubon double and an RBI from Sean Murphy, but their comeback started too late. The Cubs held on to grab the four-run win easily.
The Cubs have now won four of their last six games, and sit at 85-68 on the year. The Milwaukee Brewers have already clinched the NL Central, but the Cubs still have a two-game lead in the NL wild-card race.
The loss for the Braves dropped them to 89-64 on the season. They've still got the lead in the NL East, but by just a handful of games over the Philadelphia Phillies. A win for them on Wednesday night, along with some help from elsewhere in the league, could have clinched a postseason spot.
Both teams still have a bit of work to do to ensure a postseason berth. But the Cubs, thanks to Bregman and Crow-Armstrong, seem well on their way.

Back in April, the Boston Red Sox's season was going off the rails.
The Red Sox started the season off with a 10-17 record and opted to fire a World Series-winning manager in Alex Cora — plus a handful of other coaches — and take a gamble by turning the reins over to interim manager Chad Tracy. At the time, it seemed like the sky was falling. That's because the losses kept piling up, so much so that the Red Sox were 14 games below .500 at 32-46 on June 25.
At the time, the season looked like a disaster. The Red Sox were trending towards being sellers ahead of the trade deadline, both Roman Anthony and Garrett Crochet were on the Injured List with no end in sight, and it seemed like chief baseball officer Craig Breslow's seat was getting hotter and hotter. But the Red Sox transformed their season and now, with the season winding down, ESPN's Buster Olney reported on Wednesday that the expectation is that both Breslow and Tracy will stay on with Boston beyond the 2026 season.
"But Breslow's vision of a team succeeding with pitching and defense fully manifested, and the Red Sox are closing in on a playoff berth and will likely face the Yankees in the wild-card round, again," Olney wrote. "Manager Chad Tracy has been working under an interim tag all season, something of a head-scratcher; it may be that the two sides talked about the idea of an extension in midseason but set aside the topic for the offseason. But Boston is now expected to retain both Breslow and Tracy."
The Red Sox Are Making The Right Call
This is undoubtedly the right call for the Red Sox at this time.
Let's start with Breslow. Whether you love him or not, he has built a team that can go on a run. Sure, there have been some misses over the last few years. Losing Alex Bregman was a public relations disaster. Not landing one of the big free agent bats, including Kyle Schwarber and Pete Alonso, this past offseason also was a surprise. But there are far more wins under Breslow's belt, than losses.
Sonny Gray is going to get Cy Young Award votes and has been Boston's ace this season. Ranger Suárez was an All-Star. Willson Contreras was an All-Star. Caleb Durbin is the heart and the soul of the 2026 Red Sox. Now, the Red Sox have an All-Star catcher on their hands in Adley Rutschman. Bringing back Mickey Gasper has turned into a game-changing move. And the list goes on. The Red Sox have a roster that can make noise.
On the Tracy front, there was obviously a learning curve to being a big league manager taking over during a season, especially in such a high-profile market, like Boston. He has handled the role with grace and has clearly gotten better as the year has gone on. Plus, it doesn't hurt that the Red Sox went on a historic 15-game winning streak and put together one of the best mid-season turnarounds in MLB history. All in all, these two should both be back in 2026 and it sounds like that will be the reality.

Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman seems to impact winning everywhere he goes.
That's one of the main reasons the Boston Red Sox wanted to re-sign the two-time World Series champion and three-time All-Star.

"In addition to the typically Bregman-esque defense at the hot corner (+8 Outs Above Average) and an OPS+ more than 20% better than league average, the Cubs’ veteran offseason addition has been lauded for his clubhouse presence," MLB.com's Anthony Castrovince wrote.
"The mentorship he provided Pete Crow-Armstrong early in the year about plate approach and swing decisions helped unleash PCA’s MVP-worthy year," Castrovince added.
Whatever Bregman told Crow-Armstrong has clearly worked.

The outfielder's chase rate remains below league average, but PCA's improved swing decisions have helped him become one of the best hitters in baseball.
Clearly, Bregman deserves some credit for helping "unleash" one of the game's top stars.

When the Boston Red Sox made some additions to their starting rotation last winter, they were hoping to rebuild it around ace Garrett Crochet. Little did they know that making those moves would turn out to be monster moves.
After losing out on Alex Bregman in free agency to the Chicago Cubs, Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow pivoted to pitching. He signed left-hander Ranger Suárez of the Philadelphia Phillies. Earlier in the offseason, Breslow acquired veteran Sonny Gray from the St. Louis Cardinals.
That is turning into the biggest offseason addition made by Boston. He is going to finish at least in the top 5 in the American League Cy Young voting, but will be a free agent following the season with an option for 2027. Breslow and Gray will have a decision to make this winter, according to Kerry Miller of Bleacher Report.
Boston Red Sox Facing Sonny Gray Decision This Winter
When decisions are to be made for 2027, Gray has a mutual option of $30 million. Now, whether or not Gray plays next season remains to be seen, according to Alex Speier of the Boston Globe.
“If my family wants me to hang it up, I’ll be done in a heartbeat,” Gray said, per Speier.
If they don’t want him to retire, the Red Sox would love to have him back. He is 17-5 in his first season in Boston with a 2.76 ERA in 27 starts. He has been a workhorse in 156.2 innings with 140 strikeouts. Gray has struggled in recent outings. However, he is still on track to get the ball in Game 1 of the AL wild-card series.
“Even with major money committed to Ranger Suárez and Garrett Crochet in the rotation already, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow will probably pick up the team’s half of the option,” Miller wrote.
“The question is whether Gray will. Considering he’ll pitch next season at 37, he’s probably not going to get more than $30 million for 2027 as a free agent. However, if he declines the option, the Red Sox will owe him a $10 million buyout. So he could collect that buyout, try to get at least $20 million for 2027, and perhaps pursue a multi-year commitment. He has plenty to consider.”
Crochet has been out injured for a majority of this season and is looking for a postseason return. Suárez has been better in his last couple of starts in September.
Boston Red Sox Facing Key Offseason Decision
Gray is scheduled to make his next start on Thursday night against the Texas Rangers in Arlington. Then he’ll get one more next week before his start in the wild-card round. Depending on how far the Red Sox go, all eyes could turn to 2027.
Boston’s rotation next season, if healthy when the season begins, with Gray, could be one of the top ones in the American League. If there is any question as to whether or not Gray has another year left in him, that should have been answered by his 2026 season.
There are some big decisions coming for Breslow this winter. Gray is going to be at the top of that list.
